title: The political authority of conspiratorial claims
text:
The actual argument
The visual grammar above — the eye, the red thread, the redaction, the shouting — is the object of study, not the method. Conspiratorial claims arrive wrapped in it and are stripped of it somewhere in transit. I call that laundering, and I treat it as a mechanism to be tested rather than a label to apply.
Three transformations are coded separately, because they occur independently: the wording changes; the messenger changes; the attributed origin changes. A fourth code, the allegation itself being altered, is not laundering.

title: Theory
text:
PLACEHOLDER. Drafted with AI assistance and not yet written or verified by me. To be rewritten.



Two documents anchor the project.

The gap in the literature: what the field has established at each stage, what competes with the model, and what remains untested.
Transmission framework: the four stages as hypotheses, three routes into the intermediary, the decomposition of laundering, the cohort logic, and the falsification table.


Mechanism, rivals, and disconfirmation
Mechanism. Attributing a claim to grassroots origin lowers the reputational cost of advancing it, for elites and for the citizens who tolerate them, by signaling that the claim is already socially validated and that endorsing it is responsiveness rather than invention.
Rivals. Persuasion: attribution moves acceptance only through belief. Partisan usefulness: acceptance tracks what the claim does for the respondent’s side regardless of attribution. Authenticity (Hahl, Kim & Zuckerman Sivan 2018): a lying elite reads as authentic to voters who see the system as illegitimate. Responsiveness without concealment: “I’m responding to constituents” works even when the fringe source is fully visible.
What would force revision. A null on the grassroots-vs-elite origin contrast with adequate power; acceptance and belief moving together with a direct test of the difference null; a corpus in which elites rarely assert provenance at all.

title: Sampling rule (draft, to preregister)
text:
PLACEHOLDER. Drafted with AI assistance and not yet written or verified by me. To be rewritten.



Window: 1 September to 15 October 2024.
Fringe sources: (a) the 500 most central English-language chats in the USC Telegram 2024 dataset, by the authors’ chat-network centrality; (b) /pol/ via the 4plebs archive.
Enumeration: for each week in the window, draw a random sample of n threads from /pol/ and n messages from the selected Telegram chats. Apply the case definition to every sampled passage. Deduplicate into claim variants. Record sampling probabilities.
Elite-first claims: apply the same case definition to a random sample of Trump Truth Social posts and Factba.se transcripts in the window; enroll qualifying claims in a separate elite cohort. Do not pool the two cohorts.
Follow-up: search every enrolled claim across the intermediary corpus (Tenet transcripts; YouTube auto-captions for two named shows) and the elite corpus (Truth Social, Factba.se, Congressional Record) through 15 November 2024. Record: first qualifying appearance per tier; “no appearance in complete coverage”; “coverage incomplete”; “censored at end of follow-up.”
Decision gates (pilot): at least 40 claim variants enumerated; second-coder agreement on same-allegation judgments acceptable; count of elite adoption events reported before any modeling decision.

title: How Conspiratorial Claims Acquire Political Authority: A Gap in the Literature
text: PLACEHOLDER. Drafted with AI assistance and not yet written or verified by me. To be rewritten.

title: How Conspiratorial Claims Acquire Political Authority: A Gap in the Literature
text:
The question and the model
This dissertation asks under what conditions political elites adopt conspiratorial claims circulating outside established institutions, and whether the origin attributed to such a claim affects its political acceptability independently of its content and its endorser. I approach it through a four-stage sequence: fringe origin (imageboards such as 4chan/pol), spread through alt-media (Rumble, long-form podcasts, Telegram), elite uptake, and non-uniform electorate response. The sequence is a hypothesis, not an organizing assumption. The literature reviewed below already documents claims that begin with elites, claims assembled jointly by elites and audiences, and claims that never reach elites, and a design that cannot represent those cases cannot test the pathway. The gap this review identifies is bounded. It is not that transmission, elite amplification, or heterogeneous response are unstudied; each is. It is that, within the population of claims circulating in the U.S. alt-media ecosystem, no located study explains which claims elites select against a comparison set of claims they did not, or tests whether attributed origin moves political acceptance separately from belief.

title: How Conspiratorial Claims Acquire Political Authority: A Gap in the Literature
text:
Origin: “legitimacy” is five constructs
Barkun (2003; 2016) supplies the anchor: conspiracy theories as “stigmatized knowledge,” rejected by truth-validating institutions and “mainstreamed” when fringe and center merge. He offers a category, not a measure, and no located study follows the same claims over time and dates that crossing. Adjacent work measures adjacent things. Buehling, Zhang, and Heft (2026), comparing New World Order and Great Replacement discourse across 4chan, Twitter, and alternative news media over 2011–2021, find both platform-specific styles and convergence in how conspiracism is expressed, without identifying what drives a platform’s boundary to move. Ekman (2022) shows replacement claims being rebuilt for mainstream-right audiences, so what crosses is an argument structure, not a verbatim proposition. Pyrhönen, Bauvois, Berg, and Holley (2026), in 1,612 life-course interviews, find unprompted conspiracy talk in a tenth of transcripts and that its pandemic-era rise came substantially from passages challenging conspiracy theories. Visibility is not acceptance.
Two literatures outside conspiracy research bear directly on what “acceptance” means. Bursztyn, Egorov, and Fiorin (2020) show that shifting perceptions of public support changed willingness to express xenophobic views and the sanctions attached to doing so. Muirhead and Rosenblum (2019) describe a “new conspiracism” that works by repetition and social validation (“a lot of people are saying”) rather than by evidence, with consequences for political standing and institutions rather than for belief. Both are close precursors to the argument here, and both are theoretical or adjacent in domain. The origin stage therefore has to keep separate at least five constructs the conspiracy literature conflates as “legitimacy”: institutional endorsement, elite political endorsement, reduced social stigma, public visibility, and perceived credibility. The dissertation’s contribution beyond Bursztyn et al. and Muirhead and Rosenblum is to specify what conspiratorial content, intermediary transformation, and attributed provenance add to their mechanisms, and to test propositions that both leave untested.

title: How Conspiratorial Claims Acquire Political Authority: A Gap in the Literature
section: Spread: what intermediaries do to a claim
text:
Spread: what intermediaries do to a claim
The second stage asks what happens to a claim between its first appearance and its arrival in elite speech. The computational literature has answered the descriptive half of that question. Zannettou et al. (2018) estimated cross-platform influence among 4chan/pol, Reddit, Twitter, and Gab with Hawkes processes on hashed image memes, and coverage has since reached the platforms this model names: Telegram forwarding (Hoseini et al. 2024), Rumble podcast transcripts (Balci et al. 2025), and political podcasts, where election-fraud claims appeared in more than a quarter of episodes from 79 major shows between the 2020 election and January 6 (Wirtschafter 2023). The unit of analysis has moved from memes and links to text: Hanley and Durumeric (2024a) apply Hawkes modeling to paragraph-level embeddings across 732 Telegram channels, and Gerard, Luceri, Blas, and Ferrara (2026) build platform-invariant discourse networks from 5.7 million posts across X, TikTok, Truth Social, and Telegram during the 2024 election, predict cross-platform narrative emergence days ahead with Springfield as a demonstration, and have announced an extension to podcasts (USC Viterbi, 24 June 2026). Heft and Buehling (2022) have already set out the choice between reference-based and content-based diffusion measurement and the risks of selecting predefined actors and topics. That a claim moves across platforms, and roughly how fast, is established.
What is not established is what the claim is when it arrives. Every study above measures whether a narrative reappears, not how it changed on the way. Ekman (2022) shows in the Great Replacement case that intermediaries rebuild the argument for a new audience, but as a single-case reading, not as a coded comparison across many claims. And no located study includes elite speech as a node, so none can say whether the version an elite adopts is the fringe version, the podcast version, or something assembled at the point of adoption. Gerard et al.’s own result cuts the same way: adoption is predictable from network proximity even without direct cross-platform influence, which means reappearance can be forecast while transmission remains unidentified, and first observed appearance is not authorship.
That is the job of stage two in this dissertation. The corpus is coded at the level of the proposition (alleged conspirators, covert action, purpose, evidence offered, speaker stance, and any attributed source), and each claim’s successive versions are compared. The question is whether intermediaries supply evidence, strip stigmatized language, alter the alleged conspiracy, or attribute the claim to a source other than where it was first observed. The last of these is where stage two feeds the rest of the model: if podcasts and alt-media are where “people are saying” gets attached to claims, then asserted provenance is manufactured at this stage, elite selection at stage three can be tested against which transformed version was available, and the experiment at stage four tests a cue that the corpus shows is actually in circulation.

title: How Conspiratorial Claims Acquire Political Authority: A Gap in the Literature
section: Elite uptake: the literature already argues against a one-way pipeline
text:
Elite uptake: the literature already argues against a one-way pipeline
Here prior work competes rather than leaves a gap. Starbird, DiResta, and DeButts (2023) reconstruct three 2020 voter-fraud rumors and find “participatory disinformation”: elites set a frame, ordinary users supply apparent evidence, intermediaries select and reframe it, elites amplify the result. Benkler et al. (2020), on 55,000 stories, five million tweets, and 75,000 Facebook posts, conclude the mail-in fraud campaign was led by elites and mass media with social media in support. Bergmann (2025) argues strategic weaponization from above. Uscinski et al. (2022) find no systematic increase in aggregate conspiracy belief across their measures, which does not show supply is inconsequential but does mean any supply-side claim must be about which claims, which believers, and which elites, not about more belief overall. On the elite side, Blackington and Cayton (2025) code a decade of Polish Law and Justice speech into dog-whistles and open “barks,” and Blackington and Cayton (2024) find, against the elite-cue literature, that ruling-party tweets endorsing conspiracy theories earned less engagement than non-official ones and that threat frames, not elite identity, drove longevity. Elite endorsement does not uniformly confer an advantage, which is relevant to selection even though explaining engagement is not explaining an elite’s first adoption.
What none of this answers is selection. Why do some circulating claims receive elite endorsement while comparable claims stall? Showing that an ordinary user posted first establishes neither that the elite felt compelled to adopt it (audience capture), nor that the elite chose it to fit a prior frame (strategic selection), nor that the elite had solicited such material (joint production). Answering that requires a sample of claims identified independently of whether they became prominent, including claims first observed with grassroots users, with intermediaries, and with elites, and including claims that failed to cross a stage. A trace that starts from elite speech and works backward selects on the outcome. Springfield, documented step by step by NewsGuard, NBC, and ABC, still exists only as journalism and as a demonstration case, and any analysis of it needs stalled comparison cases beside it.

title: How Conspiratorial Claims Acquire Political Authority: A Gap in the Literature
section: Response: factual backfire is unreliable; provenance and acceptance are untested
text:
Response: factual backfire is unreliable; provenance and acceptance are untested
Factual backfire is not a reliable general expectation. Wood and Porter (2019) found none across 52 issues and 10,100 subjects; Prike, Blackley, Swire-Thompson, and Ecker (2023) found none on rating-scale measures in three experiments, with a measure-dependent exception on an open-ended response designed to elicit it; Nyhan (2021) concedes it is rare. The model should rest on non-uniform belief movement, for which there is direct evidence: Berlinski et al. (2023) show fraud allegations reduced election confidence particularly among Republicans; Lyons and Workman (2022) show explicit fraud cues raise co-partisan belief while depressing confidence broadly, and implicit cues do nothing; Radnitz (2022) finds official conspiracy claims had little effect in Georgia and Kazakhstan once motivated reasoning was accounted for. Fahey (2023) matters for how the belief measure is read: accuracy-oriented treatments failed to reduce endorsement of 2020-election and COVID misperceptions among Republicans and in one condition increased it, so reported belief is substantially sincere. Any argument that acceptance moves separately from belief has to be compatible with that.
On origin and acceptance, the nearest studies are close but not on target. Bram (2021) shows experimentally that official legitimization of a formerly fringe claim (the 2021 UFO report) warmed attitudes toward conspiracy theorists; this is the closest precursor to a normalization argument, and the expectation that attributed origin shifts acceptance is derived from it, though attitudes toward believers are not permission for politicians to advance a claim. Connor Desai and Reimers (2023) vary whether misinformation is explained as deliberate or accidental and find no difference, which concerns the falsehood’s cause, not its authorship. No located experiment holds claim and endorser constant while randomizing attributed origin, and none measures political acceptance separately from belief. Those are distinct constructs, and acceptance itself needs decomposing: permission to investigate, permission to assert publicly, willingness to excuse an unsupported assertion, and support for acting on it are different, and a respondent endorsing free inquiry is not endorsing the allegation.

title: How Conspiratorial Claims Acquire Political Authority: A Gap in the Literature
text:
Three meanings of origin
The review to this point, and the four-stage model itself, slide between three things. Documented provenance is where a claim’s development can actually be traced. Asserted provenance is where elites and intermediaries say it came from. Perceived provenance is where an audience thinks it came from. These diverge: an elite-originated claim can be presented as something ordinary people discovered, and audiences can infer grassroots origin with no explicit cue. Muirhead and Rosenblum’s title is asserted provenance as rhetoric. This distinction connects the chapters. The observational chapter codes how speakers attribute claims (to citizens, experts, anonymous sources, other elites) as part of the text already being coded, which also establishes whether provenance cues occur often enough outside an experiment to matter. The experiment tests whether those attributions move acceptance while holding the allegation, stated evidence, and apparent breadth of public support constant.

title: How Conspiratorial Claims Acquire Political Authority: A Gap in the Literature
section: Two problems any answer must survive
text:
Two problems any answer must survive
First, identification. Shojaie and Fox (2022) lay out why predictive time-series relationships are not causal; regime changes masquerade as Hawkes self-excitation (Filimonov and Sornette 2015); unobserved subprocesses create spurious cross-platform edges (Jin and Huang 2026). A finding that 4chan “led” a podcast is, without a control for the offline event that moved both, consistent with both reacting to the same cable segment, which is why causal weight cannot rest on transmission modeling. Second, the conspiratorial specificity question. A committee member will ask whether the same result would follow for any unverified accusation or partisan message. The experiment therefore needs a non-conspiratorial accusation arm, and the theory needs to say why allegations of covert coordination should behave differently from ordinary accusations of incompetence. A third, forward-looking problem: Hanley and Durumeric (2024b) estimate machine-generated articles grew sharply on small misinformation sites after ChatGPT’s release, and Costello et al. (2026, preprint) show language-model dialogues can increase as well as decrease conspiracy belief, so a human fringe incubator is an assumption to defend.

title: How Conspiratorial Claims Acquire Political Authority: A Gap in the Literature
section: Mechanism, rivals, and what would force revision
text:
Mechanism, rivals, and what would force revision
The central mechanism: attributing a claim to grassroots origin lowers the reputational cost of advancing it, for elites and for the citizens who tolerate them, by signaling that the claim is already socially validated and that endorsing it is responsiveness rather than invention. This predicts that grassroots attribution raises political acceptance more than it raises belief, that the effect is larger among co-partisans and among respondents high in perceived social sanction, and that elites attribute claims to citizens more often when the claim is stigmatized.
Two serious rivals. Persuasion: attribution moves acceptance only through belief, because “many people say it” is treated as evidence; if so, acceptance and belief move together and the difference between them is not distinguishable from zero. Partisan usefulness: acceptance tracks what the claim does for the respondent’s side regardless of attribution; if so, the origin manipulation does nothing once partisan alignment is controlled, and the observational chapter finds elites attribute claims to citizens no more often when stigmatized than when not.
Three findings that would force revision. If the C-versus-D contrast (grassroots versus elite origin, endorsement held constant) is null on acceptance with adequate power, the provenance mechanism fails and the dissertation becomes a study of selection alone. If acceptance and belief move together and a direct test of the difference is null, the normalization framing gives way to persuasion. If the coded corpus shows elites rarely assert provenance at all, the cue is not part of political rhetoric and the experiment measures a counterfactual, not a practice. The pilot exists to see the third before the other two are built.

title: Transmission framework: theory and methods by stage
text: PLACEHOLDER. Drafted with AI assistance and not yet written or verified by me. To be rewritten.

title: Transmission framework: theory and methods by stage
section: 0. The claim, stated as something that can be wrong
text:
0. The claim, stated as something that can be wrong
Among conspiratorial allegations circulating on the fringe in a given window, the ones that reach elite political speech are disproportionately those that were transformed by an intermediary in three specific ways: the allegation survived, the attributed source was obscured, and the stigmatized wording was replaced. Obscuring the source raises the political acceptability of the claim more than it raises belief in it. Each clause is a separate test with a separate way to fail.



Figure 1. The four stages are hypotheses about sequence, not assumptions. The intermediary stage can be reached by at least three routes that look identical in a cross-platform timeline (fringe first, mainstream later), which is why the design needs cohort data with identities and matched cases, not only timing.

title: Transmission framework: theory and methods by stage
text:
1. Fringe origin: enumerate, don’t select
The methodological problem at stage 1 is not tracing; it is sampling. If the claim list comes from fact-checkers, prior literature, or elite speech traced backward, the cohort is selected on visibility or on the outcome. The fix is an enumeration rule applied to the fringe corpus before anything downstream is examined.

Three ways to enumerate claims from a fringe corpus










Method
What it produces
Strength
Weakness




Manual reading of a random thread sample (pilot)
A list of distinct allegations of covert coordination, one row each
No tooling; you learn the material; the case definition gets sharpened by contact with real posts
Doesn’t scale past a few weeks; coder fatigue; needs a second coder for reliability


Semantic objects (Keim et al. 2026: Word2Vec per corpus, HDBSCAN, recursive sub-clustering)
Dense regions of meaning with no anchor list; each region is a candidate claim family
Outcome-independent by construction; gives HAD/CSD/LO metrics for later stages
Needs a large corpus per space; unstable on small corpora (Gonen et al. 2020); finds themes more than propositions


Actant narrative graphs (Tangherlini et al. 2020, PLOS ONE; Holur et al. INCANT/TAMPA)
Actors as nodes, alleged relationships as edges; a narrative framework per corpus and window
Closest to your unit (who did what to whom); designed for conspiracy narratives; handles fragmentation
Heavy NLP pipeline; entity resolution on /pol/ is ugly; requires validation of extracted relations


LLM extraction with a case definition
Structured tuples: conspirators, covert action, purpose, evidence, stance, asserted source
Directly yields the coding scheme; cheap at scale; open-weight models are competitive for this (arXiv 2605.19275)
Must be validated against human coding on a held-out sample; prompt drift; hallucinated relations





Recommended: LLM extraction with a written case definition, validated by double-coded samples, with Keim-style semantic objects as a robustness check that the extracted claims correspond to real dense regions of discourse. Process tracing is not an enumeration method; it is what you do to a handful of cases after the cohort exists.



The case definition (the part epidemiologists get right)
Epidemiology starts with a case definition that can be applied without knowing the outcome. Yours: a passage counts as a conspiratorial claim if it asserts that identifiable actors are secretly coordinating an action for a hidden purpose. Allegations of incompetence, ordinary rumor without covert coordination, and criticism of policy are excluded. Write it before coding; report how often coders disagree on the boundary.
“First observed appearance” is what the data give you. It is not authorship. Report it as first observed, and treat elite-first claims as part of the cohort rather than as errors.

title: Transmission framework: theory and methods by stage
text:
2. Intermediaries: what laundering means operationally
“Laundering” is a metaphor used by Hemmer, Starbird (2017), and Keim et al. It needs to be broken into components that can vary independently, because they do.



Figure 2. Three transformations that can occur separately or together between a fringe version and an elite version of the same allegation. A broadcaster can legitimize a claim while openly naming its fringe source (B without C). Rewording can happen with the messenger held constant (A without B). Coding them separately is what lets the design say which one does the work.



Coding sheet, per claim, per appearance









Field
Values
Used for




Claim tuple
conspirators, covert action, purpose, evidence
Deciding whether it’s the same allegation (test 1)


Tier and date
fringe / intermediary / elite; timestamp
Sequence; first-observed tier


Speaker identity
account, host, writer, guest, known pseudonyms
Detecting the personnel route


Stance
endorse / raise as concern / neutral quote / reject
Adoption is endorse or raise-as-concern only; Pyrhönen et al. show visibility often comes from challenge


Asserted provenance
named fringe source / “people are saying” / anonymous reports / constituents / expert / other elite / none
Test 2 (source obscured)


Wording register
explicit / coded / euphemistic; stigmatized terms present (0/1)
Transformation A


Constituency frame
present / absent
Responsiveness justification


Evidence of transmission
explicit citation / link / distinctive borrowed detail / chronology only
Separating sequence from borrowing






Measuring “the allegation survived” with embeddings
Keim et al. vary time; you vary tier. Train one embedding space per large corpus (fringe; intermediary transcripts), align them, and compute their three distances for each claim family. Laundering predicts low CSD (meaning preserved) with low lexical overlap (vocabulary replaced) from fringe to intermediary. Stalled claims should not show this pattern. The elite corpus is too small for its own Word2Vec space; use sentence embeddings for claim matching there and reserve the diachronic metrics for the two large tiers.









Keim metric
What it measures
Laundering prediction (fringe to intermediary)




HAD
Old associations weaken
High: stigmatized associations drop


CSD
Core meaning moves
Low: same allegation


NCD
Neighborhood fragments
Any


Lexical overlap
Same words used
Low: vocabulary replaced




That combination (HAD high, CSD low, LO low) is Keim’s “semantic narrowing with lexical replacement.” It is laundering measured in their terms. Run the Gonen et al. nearest-neighbor stability check because Procrustes alignment is seed-sensitive.

title: Transmission framework: theory and methods by stage
section: The cohort: the massive corpus question
text:
The cohort: the massive corpus question
You do not need a massive corpus of conspiracy theories. You need a bounded, complete cohort for one window, built by a rule, where most members fail. Think of it as a surveillance system for one region and one season, not a registry of every case ever.



Figure 3. Everything to the left of the vertical line happens before anyone looks at what became of a claim. The three fates on the right are the dependent variable. The middle fate matters: claims that were laundered by an intermediary and still not adopted are what separate “laundering happened” from “laundering caused adoption.”



Scale, honestly

Two weeks of /pol/ hand-read (pilot): 40 to 60 claim variants. Enough to see whether the pattern exists. Not enough for a model.
One election season, fringe + five shows + fixed elite list, LLM-extracted and validated: a few hundred variants and, realistically, 20 to 60 elite adoption events. That is a small event-history dataset; the model will be thin and the paired process tracing will carry weight.
Nothing here requires the 169M-comment scale of Keim et al. Their scale serves embedding stability on one platform over a decade. Your question is about one season across tiers.

title: Transmission framework: theory and methods by stage
section: 3. Elite adoption: selection among available claims
text:
3. Elite adoption: selection among available claims
Structure: claim × elite × week panel. Row exists while elite i has not yet adopted claim j. Outcome is first adoption in week t. Discrete-time event history (logit), elite and week fixed effects, standard errors clustered by claim. Week fixed effects absorb the shared news shocks that make Hawkes and Granger designs unreliable here.
Covariates lagged one to two weeks: fringe volume; intermediary coverage; whether a laundered version exists yet (A, B, C coded separately); prior adoption by other elites; compatibility with the elite’s prior frames; issue salience. The laundering hypothesis is the coefficient on “source-obscured version exists” holding “allegation preserved” constant. Pair the model with four to six matched cases (adopted vs stalled, same family, similar prior visibility) coded for the three routes in Figure 1.

title: Transmission framework: theory and methods by stage
section: 4. Electorate: acceptance is not belief, and rhetoric is not either
text:
4. Electorate: acceptance is not belief, and rhetoric is not either
Two things the design refuses to conflate. First, online rhetoric is not public belief; the observational chapters measure what was said, by whom, and in what form, and make no claim about what audiences believe. Second, belief is not acceptance. The literature’s baseline (roughly a tenth of Americans volunteer conspiracy talk unprompted; stable aggregate belief over time) is a scope condition, not an outcome to explain. The outcome at stage 4 is whether it becomes acceptable for a politician to advance a claim, and whether attributed origin moves that.
Experiment A: same allegation, 2×2 (original vs intermediary wording) × (earlier source hidden vs disclosed), politician and endorsement held constant. The estimand is the interaction. Experiment B: attributed authorship (citizens / campaign staff / unspecified) × politician’s justification (responding to constituents / own judgment). Measure belief, political acceptance, sanction, investigation, and circulation separately; predefine an equivalence margin for belief; define skeptics by baseline belief. Pilot in a student pool; confirmatory via TESS or a quota sample.

title: Transmission framework: theory and methods by stage
text:
The epidemiology analogy, used carefully
Tangherlini’s earlier vaccine-narrative work was published in JMIR Public Health and Surveillance, so the analogy has precedent. It is useful for design discipline and misleading as a model of mechanism.



Figure 4. What transfers from epidemiology is discipline about case definitions, denominators, and the difference between exposure and outcome. What does not transfer is the mechanism: claims are not pathogens, transmission is often deliberate, and “reproduction number” style modeling would import assumptions (homogeneous mixing, passive transmission) that Figure 1 says are false.



On training an LLM “to be an epidemiologist”
Don’t train a model; write a protocol and have a model apply it. The useful part of the idea is the surveillance frame: a fixed case definition, fixed sources, fixed window, and a model that reads every passage and flags cases. That is exactly the LLM extraction step in stage 1, and open-weight models handle it. The part to drop is the disease-dynamics modeling (SIR, R0); it assumes passive, homogeneous spread, and your Figure 1 says spread here is selective, often deliberate, and sometimes carried by one person between two rooms. Keep the vocabulary of surveillance; leave the epidemic curves.

title: Transmission framework: theory and methods by stage
section: Falsifiability and reproducibility, in one table
text:
Falsifiability and reproducibility, in one table










Test
Prediction if the theory is right
Result that forces revision
Reproducible because




1. Allegation survives
Adopted claims keep conspirators/action/purpose across tiers
Elites mostly adopt rebuilt allegations: the theory is about assembly, not transmission
Case definition, coding sheet, and validation sample are published; embedding metrics follow Keim et al.


2. Source obscured predicts adoption
Positive coefficient on “source-obscured version exists,” holding survival constant
Null or negative with adequate events: laundering is not what elites select on
Cohort built by a stated sampling rule; panel and code released


3. Obscuring moves acceptance more than belief
Wording × disclosure interaction on acceptance; belief within equivalence margin
Acceptance and belief move together: persuasion, not normalization; or disclosure has no effect: messenger or wording does the work
Preregistered; stimuli drawn from documented pairs in the cohort


0. Provenance cues exist in elite rhetoric at all
“People are saying” attaches disproportionately to claims with traceable fringe origin
Elites rarely assert provenance: the experiment tests a counterfactual, not a practice
Search terms and elite corpus listed; counts reported

title: Transmission framework: theory and methods by stage
text:
What to do first

Write the case definition and the coding sheet (one page, no code).
Hand-code two weeks of /pol/ from September 2024 with a second coder on a subsample; get a cohort of 40 to 60 variants and their fates. Report agreement.
Run the provenance-cue search on Trump and Vance 2024 transcripts (test 0).
Only if 1 and 2 show a pattern: build the extraction pipeline and the season-long cohort.
Pilot the acceptance measures in Bolsen’s pool in parallel; that is independent of everything above.

Sources referenced: Keim, Chandio, Khalid & Nithyanand (ICWSM 2026); Tangherlini et al. (PLOS ONE 2020); Holur et al. (INCANT/TAMPA); Gonen et al. (ACL 2020); Hemmer (Amanpour & Company, 9 June 2022); Starbird (ICWSM 2017); Pyrhönen et al. (Social Forces 2026); Muirhead & Rosenblum (2019); arXiv 2605.19275 on open-weight LLM classification.

title: Pilot: claim-tracking demonstration
text:
PLACEHOLDER. Drafted with AI assistance and not yet written or verified by me. To be rewritten before anything here is cited or shown.
The pilot cannot establish an adoption effect, separate the three causal routes statistically, or estimate an electorate treatment effect. It tests whether claims can be enumerated, matched, and followed reliably enough to justify building the full cohort.

title: Pilot: claim-tracking demonstration
text:
01 // Frozen scope
Scope is fixed before any search for successful claims. The window is a calendar-based stress test of measurement, not a random sample of 2024.







Decision
Fixed rule




Fringe frame
Retrievable r/conspiracy submissions dated 8–21 July UTC; up to 50 IDs/day by fixed hash; max 700


Eligible text
Title and body screened for an allegation of covert coordination plus a specific action; missing bodies marked unavailable, never “no allegation”


Unit
Claim ID = actors, secret coordinated action, target, purpose, time qualifiers; unknowns stored explicitly


Cohort
Enumerate all claims in the 700 posts; deduplicate before viewing elite matches; follow all if ≤60, else 60 by second fixed hash


Lookback
24 June to first sampled appearance, for prior occurrence and prior elite endorsement


Follow-up
28 days from entry; later occurrences retained separately


Intermediaries
52 Tenet records 8 July – 18 Aug, plus available weekday Anderson Cooper 360 broadcasts


Elites
Sitting members in the Congressional Record, plus sitting officeholders and major-party tickets quoted directly in the selected material



Fallback window is 17–30 June 2024, chosen only if the July access gate fails, documented before enumeration. The window is never changed because few July claims were adopted.
The 60-claim cap is a workload ceiling, not a target. Twenty well-defined claims beat sixty ambiguous topics; a low yield is retained and reported.

title: Pilot: claim-tracking demonstration
text:
03 // Method boundaries
Use an LLM to propose structured extractions and sentence embeddings to retrieve candidate matches; decide same-allegation and endorsement questions by hand. Do not fine-tune, build agent systems, fit Hawkes processes, or train aligned embeddings for this demonstration. A held-out benchmark decides which affordable model is adequate; there is no universal best model.
Population prevalence is not estimated here. Online posting, source popularity, elite rhetoric, political acceptability, and belief stay distinct variables.
